To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

browsing induced changes in the architecture of plant canopies can affect forage production, which in turn can affect population dynamics of mammalian browsers, and that the resulting feedback can result in population oscillations.

(1) browsing induced changes in the fractal dimension of plant canopies can affect forage availability to large mammalian herbives and (2) these changes in forage availability, which can be quadratic or monotonic functions of herbivore density, can feed back to alter the population dynamics of herbivores.

1) the architecture of plant crowns is altered by browsing by large mammal herbivores; 2) the architecture of tree crowns is altered in a density-dependent manner; and 3) the density-dependent changes in tree crown architecture feed back onto the population dynamics of mammalian herbivore populations.

how the structure of plant communities is altered by the foraging of large herbivores, and the consequences of these changes for the dynamics of the herbivores themselves.
